name: Page Turners
subject: Books and authors
tagline: Twenty questions on novels, novelists and the stories behind the stories. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: Who wrote the Harry Potter books?
questions.w: J. K. Rowling, who began the first book on a delayed train from Manchester to London in 1990.
questions.more: Twelve publishers turned it down before Bloomsbury took it for a 2,500-pound advance, reportedly because the chairman's eight-year-old daughter demanded the next chapter. The series has sold more than 600 million copies. The initials were her publisher's idea, to hide from boys that a woman wrote it; she has no middle name, so she borrowed her grandmother's, Kathleen.

questions.q: Which Charles Dickens story features Ebenezer Scrooge and the ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come?
questions.w: A Christmas Carol, written in six weeks in 1843 and in the shops a week before Christmas.
questions.more: Dickens paid for the lavish first edition himself and, because he priced it low, made almost nothing from it. It has never been out of print. The book is credited with reviving the English Christmas, from 'Merry Christmas' as a greeting to the turkey dinner, and 'Scrooge' entered the dictionary within a generation.

questions.q: Who created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
questions.w: Arthur Conan Doyle, a struggling Edinburgh-trained doctor, in A Study in Scarlet in 1887.
questions.more: Holmes was modelled on Doyle's medical professor Joseph Bell, who could diagnose a stranger's trade and travels at a glance. Doyle grew so sick of him that he threw him off the Reichenbach Falls in 1893; public outrage, and a large cheque, brought him back ten years later. Holmes never says 'Elementary, my dear Watson' in any of the stories.

questions.q: Which novel opens with the line 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife'?
questions.w: Pride and Prejudice, by Jane Austen, published in 1813.
questions.more: Austen's first draft, called First Impressions, was rejected by a publisher unread in 1797. She sold the copyright for 110 pounds and never saw the bulk of the profits. All her novels were published anonymously, 'by a Lady', and her name appeared on them only after her death in 1817.

questions.q: The Hunger Games trilogy is set in a future nation called what?
questions.w: Panem, from the Latin 'panem et circenses', bread and circuses.
questions.more: Suzanne Collins said the idea came from flicking between reality television and news footage of the Iraq war late one night. Gilead is the theocracy of The Handmaid's Tale, Oceania the superstate of Nineteen Eighty-Four, and Westeros the continent of Game of Thrones.

questions.q: Which 1960 novel, set in Alabama, follows the lawyer Atticus Finch through the eyes of his daughter Scout?
questions.w: To Kill a Mockingbird, by Harper Lee, which won the Pulitzer Prize the following year.
questions.more: Lee based Scout's friend Dill on her childhood neighbour Truman Capote, and she helped Capote research In Cold Blood in Kansas. She published nothing else for 55 years until Go Set a Watchman, an early draft featuring an older, racist Atticus, appeared in 2015 amid questions about whether she had really consented.

questions.q: The pen name George Orwell belonged to which writer, author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four?
questions.w: Eric Arthur Blair, who took the name from a river in Suffolk and England's patron saint.
questions.more: He was born in India, served as a colonial policeman in Burma, washed dishes in Paris and was shot through the throat fighting the fascists in Spain. He wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four while dying of tuberculosis on the Scottish island of Jura and finished it in 1948; the title may simply swap the last two digits. Samuel Clemens was Mark Twain, Charles Dodgson was Lewis Carroll and David Cornwell was John le Carré.

questions.q: Which Colombian author's One Hundred Years of Solitude follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the town of Macondo?
questions.w: Gabriel García Márquez, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.
questions.more: He wrote it in eighteen months in Mexico City while his wife pawned the car and the household appliances, and they could not afford the postage to send the whole manuscript to the publisher, so they sent half. It has sold some 50 million copies in 46 languages and is the defining work of magical realism. Netflix adapted it in 2024.

questions.q: Which Russian novelist wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina?
questions.w: Leo Tolstoy, a count who later renounced his wealth, his copyrights and most of his novels.
questions.more: His wife Sophia copied out War and Peace by hand at least seven times as he revised it. In old age he became a Christian anarchist and pacifist whose writings influenced Gandhi, with whom he corresponded. He died at 82 in a remote railway station after fleeing his home and his marriage in the middle of the night.

questions.q: Which novel by Gustave Flaubert, about a doctor's wife's affairs and debts in provincial France, got its author put on trial for obscenity in 1857?
questions.w: Madame Bovary. Flaubert was acquitted and the scandal made the book a bestseller.
questions.more: He spent five years on it, hunting for 'le mot juste', the exact word, and sometimes managed a page a week. Asked who the heroine was based on he is supposed to have said 'Madame Bovary, c'est moi'. Nana and Thérèse Raquin are by Émile Zola; Les Liaisons dangereuses is from 1782.

questions.q: Which Nigerian author's 1958 novel Things Fall Apart, about the Igbo leader Okonkwo and the arrival of missionaries, is the most widely read book in African literature?
questions.w: Chinua Achebe, who took the title from a W. B. Yeats poem.
questions.more: He wrote it in English deliberately, to answer colonial novels such as Heart of Darkness from the inside. The handwritten manuscript was nearly lost when a London typing agency ignored it for months. It has sold more than twenty million copies in some sixty languages; Achebe never won the Nobel, which many consider the prize's great omission.
